issues.title: Handshake Context for supplemental authentication is not defined
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
The draft describes transcript construction for supplemental authentication, but it does not explicitly define this in terms of the Handshake Context defined in Section 4.4 of TLS 1.3. 

The draft should explicitly define the Handshake Context used for supplemental authentication sequences.

a) The Handshake Context will differ between the client and the server, consistent with the Table in Section 4.4.
b) The Handshake Context should include the CertificateRequest message that carries the supplemental_certificate_requests extension.

Previously transmitted supplemental authentication messages would become part of the evolving Handshake Context, so that each subsequent CertificateVerify and Finished computation includes them.

Apart from the definition of the Handshake Context, the construction of CertificateVerify and Finished should follow the same rules defined in Section 4.4 of TLS 1.3.

comments.body: Good point. The text should be more explicit

issues.title: Interaction with KeyUpdate, EKU, and post-handshake client authentication
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body: We should clarify whether KeyUpdate, EKU, and post-handshake client authentication messages can interleave with supplemental authentication sequences, and whether any ordering restrictions are required.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
I think this is clarified in section 3:

> Supplemental authentication flights from a given sender MUST form a contiguous sequence of handshake messages. An endpoint MUST NOT interleave application data or other TLS messages with its supplemental authentication flights.

comments.author: tireddy2
comments.body:
> I think this is clarified in section 3:
> 
> > Supplemental authentication flights from a given sender MUST form a contiguous sequence of handshake messages. An endpoint MUST NOT interleave application data or other TLS messages with its supplemental authentication flights.

I was referring to cross-flight interleaving of messages.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: How can that happen? Are you referring to DTLS endpoint sending both supplemental certificates immediately followed by EKU, NewSessionTicket or PHA and getting UDP packets reordered? Or something else?

issues.title: Compatibility with QUIC post-handshake restrictions
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
RFC 9001 states that servers MUST NOT use post-handshake client authentication and specifically:

servers MUST NOT send post-handshake TLS CertificateRequest messages, and clients MUST treat receipt of such messages as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

Since this draft introduces additional Certificate, CertificateVerify, and Finished authentication sequences after the handshake, it is unclear how this mechanism would operate over QUIC without violating the QUIC-TLS restriction.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: QUIC-TLS prohibits Post Handshake Authentication as specified in RFC8446 because authentication context potentially changes after QUIC handshake and this change might apply to different streams differently. This proposal does not have this problem.

issues.title: Identities for subsequent authentication
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
whether multiple supplemental authentication sequences may represent the same identity using different certificate chains or present alternative identities ?

It looks like the draft is an alternative mechanism for RFC9261.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
This is intentionally not defined as both cases are within scope.

Not sure how this proposal is an alternative to exported authenticators:
- exported authenticators are sent on application layer and wrapped into application logic and framing
- exported authenticators are typically sent based on some application layer event. This proposal is strictly before application layer data is sent

issues.title: max_certificates
issues.author: rifaat-ietf
issues.body:
I was wondering about your choice of using max_certificates.

How would a server, for example, explicitly require the client to provide exactly two certificates:
A traditional certificate and PQC certificate? or 
A user certificate and a device certificate?

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
`max_certificates` applies to each `SupplementalCertificateRequest`. In your example, the server will request one client certificate via the `CertificateRequest` itself and exactly one supplemental certificate by including `supplemental_certificate_requests` with `max_certificates`=1 in the only `CertificateRequest`.

But if there are up to 3 device attestation certificates that server would like to accept from the client (in addition to user cert) it would send `CertificateRequest ` for the user cert with `supplemental_certificate_requests` extension containing one `SupplementalCertificateRequest` with `max_certificates`=3

comments.author: rifaat-ietf
comments.body:
max_certificates implies that the party that sent the request is willing to accept no certificates at all. For example, if max_certificates=1 it implies that the party is willing to accept a maximum of 1 certificate, which includes no certificate.

If this is not the intention, then maybe we need to find a better name for this parameter.
If it is intentional, then this implies that the application is required to enforce whatever policy it wants at a later stage.

Both valid, and have pros and cons.
